about: Doccinga (Dokkum) in Oostergo: the church on the martyr's mound, the creek landing and the farms around it, 793 to 1066. Written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/doccinga.md and the spine. A draft in the game's own files, for the user to overwrite. (?) marks what is not verified.

ports.summary: A wooden church on a raised mound in the salt marsh, kept as the place where Boniface and his companions were killed in 754, with a clergy house, a graveyard and a spring. South of it a long dwelling mound of stock farmers lies above a tidal creek. A merchant comes for Frisian cloth, cheese, butter and hides straight from the farms, and brings what the marsh lacks: grain, timber, iron, querns, pots, and wine and wax for the altar.
ports.seasons: The year turns on the fifth of June, Boniface's day, when the marsh fills with pilgrims and Liudger rides through; he comes again in autumn on his way to teach at Traiectum. Shearing and the new cheese come before midsummer, slaughter and hides at Martinmas, and from then until Easter the storm tides run over the unembanked marsh and the creeks are no place for a stranger.

history.text: Charles Martel beat the Frisians on the Boorne. The land west of the Lauwers has been the Franks' since.

On the fifth of June Boniface was killed with Bishop Eoba and about fifty companions. Willibald names only the river Bordne; the people here hold that it was on this ground. Fulda and Mainz count the year as 755.
history.source: Willibald, Life of Boniface ch. 8 (tr. Robinson 1916, paraphrased); dossier section 8

history.text: The killers broke open the mission's chests looking for gold, found books, and strewed them over the meadow and into the reeds, where some were found long after, unharmed.

By this year, on King Pippin's order, Count Abba and a great part of the Frisian folk had raised a mound against the spring tides. A church and a house for the clergy were built on it, and a spring of sweet water broke out where a horse sank.
history.source: Willibald ch. 9 (paraphrased); the mound is 3 to 4 m of salt-marsh sods, built in one go: Cultuurhistorische verkenning binnenstad Dokkum, 2008

history.text: Willehad, a Northumbrian priest, began his mission here some time between 765 and 774, then crossed the Lauwers, where heathens cast lots on whether he should die. He left alive.
history.source: Catholic Encyclopedia, Willehad; Allgemeine Deutsche Biographie, Willehad; the year is the middle of the range (?)

history.text: Liudger, a Frisian taught at Traiectum and York, was set over Oostergo from this church. He taught here seven years and went to Traiectum each autumn to teach there.
history.source: Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.17-21, as in the spine and the Catholic Encyclopedia, Ludger

history.text: In Widukind's rising the Frisians drove out the priests, burned churches and went back to the old gods. Whether this church burned is written nowhere (?).
Saxons and Frisians east of the Lauwers, the next river east, rose again. Churches were burned and priests driven out. Doccinga stayed quiet and took in those who fled.
history.source: chronicle_793.json 793-autumn-saxon-revolt; the fugitives here are the game's reading (?)

history.text: The king's new heavy penny was ordered to be taken in every place. The Frisian law counts its fines in old money and new.
history.source: chronicle_793.json 794-06-frankfurt-new-denier; Lex Frisionum, introduction by K. Nieuwenhuijsen, keesn.nl/lex

history.text: Liudger died on the twenty-sixth of March, bishop at Mimigernaford.
In summer two hundred Danish ships ravaged the Frisian islands. Three fights were lost and a hundred pounds of silver was paid.
On the day after Christmas a storm flood went over Frisia. 2,437 were counted drowned.

About this year Altfrid wrote his Life of Liudger, the first sure text to name this place. In the same half-century a cleric of Utrecht asked here about Boniface, and a very old woman swore she had seen the killing.
history.source: Cultuurhistorische verkenning 2008; Levison's note on the Utrecht Life, as in the dossier section 3

history.text: In June Rodulf, a baptised Dane of royal kin, demanded tribute of Oostergo. The Frisians answered that they owed it to none but King Louis and his sons. He fell with five or eight hundred men; the rest, shut in a building, bought their lives with their treasure and an oath never to return. No annal says where.
history.source: Annals of Fulda 873, Annals of St Bertin and Xanten 873, as quoted at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodulf_Haraldsson; dossier section 5

history.text: Aalsum, the mound just north, is in Fulda's list of its lands as Atlesheim.
About this year the name is written Doccinga. In this century come churches of tuff stone, the first sea dikes along the creek, a market, a toll and a mint.
The counts of Brunswick hold Oostergo, from this year or from 1006. None of them is known to have come here.
Count Bruno's silver pennies are struck here, reading DOCC and BRVN, with the king's crowned head on the other face. They are found as far off as the Baltic lands and Russia.
history.source: en.numista.com/48388 (Dannenberg 499, 501; the type is dated 1038-1057 or 1050-1057); Cultuurhistorische verkenning 2008

history.text: Count Bruno was killed on the twenty-sixth of June. Egbert followed him.

eras.text: The mission church of the bishop of Traiectum, two generations old, with its priests back after the rising of 784. No market, no toll, no mint: a church, a spring, farms and a muddy landing. East of the Lauwers the churches burn in 793 and priests come here on foot. Liudger passes each spring and autumn. Bread is dear in the hungry years and the farms pay for grain in cloth and cheese.

Liudger is dead and his feast is kept on the twenty-sixth of March beside Boniface's. In 810 the Danish fleet lies on the islands and every mound is told its share of the hundred pounds. Afterwards the church is fuller than before, the old people who saw 754 are dying, and clerks from Traiectum begin to write down what they say.

After the great flood of Christmas 838 the mounds stand in a marsh of dead cattle and new creeks, and the graveyard is larger. Danish lords hold the Rhine mouths to the south. Baptised Northmen live among the Frisians here; one of them has a farm and grandchildren. In June 873 Rodulf comes for tribute and is killed.

A quiet century by the record. The church keeps its day, Fulda holds land at Aalsum, and the clergy house is where church law is spoken for the district. Frisians of this coast carry cloth and take silver in every sea, and bring some of it home.

The name is written Doccinga. A church of grey tuff stone from the Rhine is going up for canons and pilgrims, and a small one of Saint Martin south of it for the parish. The first low sea dikes run along the creek. There is a market on the long mound and a man who takes the count's toll.

Count Bruno of Brunswick, who has never been seen here, has pennies struck in his name: small, thin, with the king's crowned head. Skippers take them north and east by the bagful. In 1057 Bruno is killed and Egbert follows. The place is a market town in all but name.

sites.name: The creek landing
sites.see: A grey mud bank below the long mound where several creeks join the sea arm that runs east to the Lauwers. Boats lie tilted on the ooze at the ebb, a line of stakes shows where the hard ground is, and behind them the church stands dark on its own mound against a wide sky. It smells of salt mud and cattle; curlews call, and the tide comes in without a sound.
sites.source: the creeks and the sea arm: Cultuurhistorische verkenning binnenstad Dokkum 2008; nothing of the landing itself has been found, so the stakes are ours (?)

sites.name: The long mound
sites.see: A long low hill of sods and dung with one path along its back, square to the water. Turf-walled houses with their byres under the same roof stand end-on to the wind, smoke seeping through the thatch. Cheeses dry on a rack, hides are pegged out on the slope, and in front a woman sells butter from a tub to whoever has come off a boat.
sites.source: the dwelling mound south of the church, its street square to the water; its age is not known and digs found nothing before the late 12th century on its west flank: Cultuurhistorische verkenning 2008 (?)

sites.name: The church of Saint Paul and Saint Boniface
sites.see: A plank church with a reed roof on the top of a steep round mound, higher than anything else to the horizon. Inside it is dim and smells of wax, wet wool and salt timber; a single lamp burns before the altar and a wooden board is cut with the names of the dead of 754. From the door the whole marsh lies open, creeks shining, as far as the sea.
sites.source: Willibald ch. 9: the church built on the mound; the dedication from Alcuin's verses (MGH Poetae I 304) as cited in Robinson's note; timber traces found 1950-1978. The board of names is ours; the names are Willibald's (?)

sites.name: The clergy house
sites.see: A long timber house on the lee side of the church mound, with a bench along its south wall where the priests sit to hear cases. Two twigs wrapped in white wool lie on a shelf inside the door, one cut with a cross. Men stand about in the wind waiting their turn, and a boy is being taught his letters on a wax board.
sites.source: the clergy's dwelling: Willibald ch. 9; later the seat of church law for the district: Cultuurhistorische verkenning 2008. The lot of two twigs, one marked with a cross, wrapped in clean wool and laid on the altar: Lex Frisionum XIV

sites.name: The spring on the mound
sites.see: A small clear pool beside the church, edged with sods, in a country where every other water is brackish. A wooden dipper hangs on a post. Women come up the path with yokes and buckets; a pilgrim kneels, drinks, and fills a little flask to carry home.
sites.source: Willibald ch. 9: Abba rode round the finished mound, a servant's horse sank to its forelegs, and a sweet spring broke out; a 9th-century Utrecht Life puts it beside the church. Perhaps a pond of the fresh water that gathers under a mound: Cultuurhistorische verkenning 2008

sites.name: The graves on the mound
sites.see: The east slope of the church mound, set with low wooden markers that lean with the wind, all the graves lying east and west. The grass is cropped short by a tethered ewe. From here the landing is in plain sight, so that the dead, people say, can see who comes home.
sites.source: burial on the mound: Cultuurhistorische verkenning 2008; Rijksmonument 47514. Aldger's father's grave is the spine's (york_blood)

sites.name: The meadow and the reeds
sites.see: Flat salt pasture beyond the creek, bitten close by small dark cattle, with a wide bed of reeds along the water that hisses when the wind gets up. Nothing marks it. People crossing it lower their voices; this, they say, is where the books lay in the grass.
sites.source: Willibald ch. 8: the books strewn over the meadow and thrown into the reeds, found long after unharmed. That it was this meadow is the people's belief, not the record (?)

sites.name: The weaving house at Aalsum
sites.see: The next mound north, bigger and older than the church's, a short walk over the marsh by a plank path. In a sunken hut with its door to the south three women stand at upright looms, beating up the weft with oak swords; the thud carries outside. Finished cloth hangs striped and checked on a pole, and the place smells of wet wool and tallow.
sites.source: Aalsum: about 4 ha, 5.3 m above the sea; finds of an oak weaving sword, a bronze cloak pin with inlaid stones and a gold ring with a red stone: nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aalsum_(Noardeast-Fryslân). The woman who weaves fresum: Lex Frisionum, judgements of Wlemar

sites.name: The Northman's farm
sites.see: A farm on a mound of its own toward the sea, built like the others but with a boat shed beside the byre and a ship's strake for a lintel. An old man sits by the door mending a net with fingers that have held other things. A wooden cross is nailed over the door and a worn hammer of bone hangs inside it.
sites.source: Annals of Fulda 873: a Northman, long a Christian and settled among the Frisians, led them against Rodulf. His farm, and that it lay here, are ours (?)

sites.name: The market on the long mound
sites.see: The path along the back of the long mound, widened and laid with planks, with booths of hurdle and sailcloth on both sides. Behind the booths rises the new church of grey tuff, half built, with hoists and ropes on it. A man with a tally stick and a small scale stands where the path meets the landing and looks into every basket.
sites.source: market and toll in the 11th century, the tuff church of Saint Boniface and Saint Paul and the small Saint Martin's: Cultuurhistorische verkenning 2008; H. M. van den Berg, dbnl. The year 1000 for the market is a round guess (?)

sites.name: Count Bruno's mint
sites.see: A small plank house with a barred door on the long mound, with a hearth, an anvil set in an oak stump and two men striking in turn. Each blow leaves a thin bright penny with a crowned head on it. A boy sweeps the floor into a pan, because the sweepings are silver too.
sites.source: Bruno's pennies, about 0.7 g and 17 mm, DOCC / BRVN / VGGA and HENRICVS RE: en.numista.com/48388. No moneyer of Dokkum is named; the house is ours

people.name: Aldger
people.trait: Steady, sparing with words, counts tides in his head; baptised as a child at this church and keeps every fast.
people.want: To see the blood-price paid at Eoforwic, so that he can walk its strand again under his own name: he was the boy on the ship that fled in 773.
people.fear: The dead youth's kin; and fog on a lee shore.
people.voice: Dry Frisian: says the worst first and plainly, then what can be done about it. At home he says even less, and looks at the graves.
people.looks: A little over thirty, broad, short-legged, sandy hair and a cropped beard, eyes narrowed from watching water; a short Frisian cloak, a wooden cross on a thong, the steering oar's callus on his right hand.
knows: every creek between the Vlie and the Lauwers, and which of them the last winter moved
who on the long mound is kin to whom
what was said aboard Radger's ship in 773, which he tells only when asked on a quiet night
where his father lies

ties.note: the same person
his mother; he sends her half of every share and she spends none of it on herself
they learned their letters on the same bench under Liudger; Aldger forgot his
each thinks he knows the creeks better
sailed for her husband Radger as a boy and still does her errands unasked
was on the ship of the man who killed Ecgwulf's brother
Liudger baptised his sisters and was on the same ship home from York
ten years on the same thwart; the Northman is the one heathen he has stopped praying about
the Vecht ferryman: two steersmen who can stand an hour together without speaking
had the Thames marks from him as a young man, and has not let them slip
gave the boy back some of the marks the old man gave him
the head of the old lords' terp knew his father, and asks every skipper whether he still sails
showed him the Lauwers channels one summer; Sicco tells it as if they were equals
knows what she would like of him, and has gone to sea about it
she knew his mother on the islands, and asks after his knee
island people both; their mothers were of one house (?)
boys on this mound together; the knife at his belt is Meinbod's work
the host at York who saw him cast off as a ship's boy in the year of the killing
tells the wright at Ganda when a boat is tired before the wright can see it
sat on her bench as a young steersman and mended her roof in a gale
compares sands with the island's pilot, his and the Frisian ones
learned the Thames marks from Gerlef as a boy, sleeping in this man's loft
gives the cellarer the worst news first, which the cellarer likes
counts tides with him; an hour's talk in twenty words

lines.greet: This is the place. The mud is worse than I told you and the cheese is better. Mind the third stake; the ground beyond it is not ground.
lines.greet_again: Home again. My mother will count your men, then feed one more than there are.
rumour: My father carried sods for that mound when he was a boy. Half the country did. He said the count rode round it like a man buying a horse.
The creek by the alders has moved a boat's length since I was here. Radbrand will say it has not. Sound it yourself.
My mother has a cloth with a knot in it. Do not ask her what is in the knot unless you mean to hear all of it.
lines.grave: He lies there, third from the thorn. He never asked me what happened at York. I think he knew, and thought asking would make it true.
lines.saying: A Frisian trusts God and the mound, and builds the mound first.
lines.farewell: The ebb turns before the lamp is lit. If we are still here then, we are here until morning.

people.source: invented; the spine's cast.crew.aldger. The flight of the Frisians from York about 773 is Altfrid, Vita Liudgeri I.11-12

people.name: Liafhild
people.trait: Small, quick, and exact about what is owed; she feeds strangers before she asks their names.
people.want: Her son clear of the blood at York before she dies, and a grandchild on the long mound.
people.fear: That Aldger will be known on some English strand and not come home; and a year with no grain boat.
people.voice: Brisk and plain, a question at the end of most things she says. She never names York; it is 'over there'.
people.looks: About fifty-five, thin and upright, grey hair under a linen cap, a striped Frisian shawl held with a bronze pin, a ring of keys at her belt and a small knotted cloth tucked beside them.
knows: the price of butter, cheese and cloth on every mound within a day's walk
who has grain in a hungry year and who only says so
the story of 773 as a boy of twelve told it the night he came home
which graves are whose

ties.note: her only living son
her son, the house's steersman
sells her butter beside Meinhild's cloth and has for thirty years
thinks Adelsuit's story grows a little every June
Radger's widow sent cloth and grain the winter Aldbrand died; it has not been paid back and neither woman has forgotten
he buried her husband and baptised her daughters

lines.greet: So you are the one he steers for. You are thinner than I thought. Sit down, the pot is on. I hope he keeps the fasts.
lines.greet_again: You again, and all of them still alive. Good. There is buttermilk, and bread if you brought the grain for it.
rumour: Twelve pennies, light ones, the old king's. A ship's boy's wage for that voyage. I have not spent one. It is not money, is it? It is a debt.
The priest says the churches burn again over the Lauwers. Two came here on foot at dusk. I gave them my husband's cloak between them.
Meinhild has a daughter of an age to marry and a chest to send with her. In a year like this, a chest is bread.
lines.wage: If the price is ever named over there, these twelve go into it first. Then let the rest be yours. Will you carry them?
lines.saying: Butter keeps a week, cloth a lifetime, a grudge three generations. Sell the butter first.
lines.farewell: Bring him back. And bring rye; I will pay in cheese, and you will have the better of it.

people.source: invented; the spine's york_blood hook for Doccinga: Aldger's mother still has the ship's boy's wage from that voyage, unspent. The pennies of the old light weight are the game's detail (?)

people.name: Meinward
people.trait: Patient and practical; a farmer's son who keeps the church's cattle as carefully as its books, and has been driven out once already.
people.want: A bell, so the marsh can hear the hours; wax and wine enough for Boniface's day; and to die in this house and not on a road.
people.fear: Smoke to the east; and the bishop's steward asking why the tithe cheese is short.
people.voice: Slow, kind, a little rustic in his Latin and knows it. He talks of Boniface as of a guest who was treated badly in his own district.
people.looks: About thirty-five, sturdy, tonsured, wind-reddened face, a dark wool tunic patched at the elbows, mud to the knee, a wax board and a horn spoon in his belt.
knows: the Frisian law as it is spoken here: wergilds, the lots, the fine for Sunday work
when Liudger is expected and by which road
the names of the fifty, by heart
what the bishop at Traiectum wants carried and what he pays
who east of the Lauwers has gone back to the old gods

ties.note: Liudger was his master here from 777 until the priests were driven out in 784
the church is the bishop of Traiectum's and so is he
the island priest lodges here on his way west and they argue about fish on fast days
boys on the same school bench
he believes her, mostly, and has told the bishop's clerks to come and hear her before she dies
people who cannot reach him for a fever cross the Lauwers to her
sends the tithe and the district's fines to Saint Martin's by any boat going south
the priest across the Vlie; they send each other oil and complaints by passing boats
a priest from beyond the Lauwers who has slept on his floor more than once
the pilot owes three years' tithe; the priest has stopped mentioning it, which works no better
the smith made the church's hinges, and is paid in Masses he mostly attends

lines.greet: A boat, and not one I know. God be thanked. I had hoped for wax. Come in anyway, the wind is the same for everyone.
lines.greet_again: The merchant. I said a prayer for your keel on Sunday. It seems to have held.
rumour: Master Liudger comes through before Boniface's day and again when the leaves turn. He walks his horse through the village. Ask him anything; he asks first.
Over the Lauwers they have burned what we built. Priests come to me with nothing but their oil. I have beds for four and there are nine.
Sunday work costs four solidi here and twelve beyond the river. So a man who must mend his net on a Sunday does well to live on this side.
lines.law: A man is killed in a crowd and no one saw. We wrap two twigs in wool, one with a cross. A boy draws. It is better than a feud.
lines.saying: He came with books and they looked for gold. People still mistake the one for the other, in both directions.
lines.farewell: Go with God, and come back before the fifth of June. I need wine that has not been watered twice.

people.source: invented; no priest of Dokkum is named in these years. Clergy of Utrecht serve the church: Cultuurhistorische verkenning 2008. The law he speaks: Lex Frisionum XIV and XVIII

people.name: Adelsuit
people.trait: Certain. She has told one story all her life and has never changed a word of it that she will admit to.
people.want: To be believed by someone who can write, before she is too old to swear.
people.fear: That it will be told wrong when she is dead; and, in the night, the sound of the reeds.
people.voice: Low and flat, the same phrases in the same order, like a thing learned by heart. She looks at the meadow while she speaks.
people.looks: In 793 about fifty, broad, weather-brown, a grey head-cloth and an undyed gown, a yoke and two buckets; by 830 bent double and nearly blind, led by a great-grandchild, one hand always on the wooden dipper at the spring.
knows: what she saw on the fifth of June when she was ten, as she tells it
where the books lay, and who picked up what
which families crossed the boundary three days later and what they brought back
the weather by her knees

ties.note: he listens every time as if it were the first
two widows of one mound, one story between them
her sister's son; she does not speak of his father's people
he heard her out in his seven years here and wrote nothing down, which she holds against him gently
a tenant of Saint Martin's; her rent is paid in cheese

lines.greet: You are standing where the tents were. I was ten. I had come to see the bishop put his hands on my brothers. Sit, and I will tell it.
lines.greet_again: You came back. Most hear it once. Sit; I will begin where I stopped.
lines.greet_old: Who is it? The merchant's voice. Good. A clerk is coming from the bishop to write it down. You will stand by and hear me swear.
rumour: When the sword came down he held a book over his head. A gospel book. I saw the blade go into it. I have never said otherwise.
They drank his wine and fought each other over chests they had not opened. When they opened them it was books. I heard them shouting at the books.
Three days after, the Christians came over the boundary and killed a great many, and took the women and children. Some families here began that week.
lines.saying: I do not say what I think. I say what I saw.
lines.farewell: Tell it as I told it. Not better.

people.source: A very old woman who swore, to a cleric of Utrecht in the first half of the 9th century, that she saw Boniface cover his head with a gospel book: the Utrecht Life, in Levison's edition p. 73, as in Robinson's note. She is real and has no name in the source: the name Adelsuit (Adel- + -suit), her birth year and her kin are ours (?)

people.name: Radbrand
people.trait: Sour, exact and funny without smiling; baptised like everyone, and unimpressed by it.
people.want: To be paid for what he knows, and for strangers to stop asking him to show them the holy meadow for nothing.
people.fear: The winter flood that takes the cattle; and that his grandfather's part in 754 will be said aloud on a feast day.
people.voice: Short, sideways, a price in every second sentence. He answers a pious remark with a remark about mud.
people.looks: Near forty, long and stooped, a face like split oak, bare feet black with creek mud, a sounding pole twice his height, a short cloak that Franks laugh at and he does not.
knows: the creeks to the Lauwers mouth and the hour each one drains
which skippers have come and gone this month and what they carried
where the Danes' ships were last seen off the islands
who on the mounds has cattle to sell quietly

ties.note: his mother's sister; he fetches her water and lets her think he believes all of it
Aldger went to sea and thinks that is the same as knowing the creeks
three years' tithe of his pilot's pennies, which the priest has stopped mentioning
the Maas pilot; they met once at Dorestad and spent a night agreeing that skippers are fools
takes people over the Lauwers to her for fevers and says nothing to the priest
the Ems pilot; they trade word of where the channels went after each winter
the smith mends his boat hooks, and is told which boats are coming

lines.greet: You came in on the wrong creek. It worked, so now you will think it is the right one. A penny, and I show you the other.
lines.greet_again: Still afloat. Then you listened, or you were lucky. I charge the same for both.
rumour: A Frank told me my cloak was too short to cover a man in bed. I said in this country a long cloak is a wet cloak.
A boat from the islands says there are sails off the north shore that are nobody's kin. I would not lie out there overnight.
Pilgrims ask me where he died. I show them the meadow. The priest shows them the mound. Both are a short walk, so nobody complains.
lines.saying: The sea gives the land in the morning and wants it back by evening. Do your business at noon.
lines.farewell: Go out on the last of the flood, not the first of the ebb. They are not the same, whatever your steersman says.

people.source: invented; no pilot is recorded. The Frisians' short cloaks that the king complained of: Notker, Gesta Karoli I.34 (tr. Grant 1907), paraphrased

people.name: Meinhild
people.trait: Proud of her hands and careful of them; she drives a hard bargain slowly and remembers every piece she ever sold.
people.want: A good match for her daughter Thiadhild and a buyer who comes back each year, so she need not sell to whoever lands.
people.fear: A hungry winter that eats the dowry chest; and a blow to her hand.
people.voice: Unhurried, to the beat of the loom. She speaks of cloth as other people speak of kin.
people.looks: Mid-forties, tall, strong forearms, fair hair braided and pinned up out of the warp, a checked gown of her own weaving, an oak weaving sword in her hand and a bronze pin set with small stones at her shoulder.
knows: the grades of Frisian cloth and what each fetches at Dorestad and over the sea
which dyes hold and which run
who is marrying whom from here to Winaldum
that the law puts a quarter more on a blow to a weaver's hand, and why

ties.note: thirty years side by side on market days
would not mind him for a son-in-law and has said so to everyone but him
Thiadburg's storehouse at Dorestad takes her best cloth when a boat is going
his man came, felt the cloth, and offered half; she has not forgotten the offer or the feeling
the weaver of the old lords' mound; each has handled the other's cloth at Dorestad and found one fault in it

lines.greet: Feel it before you ask the price. No, with the back of the hand. Now you may ask.
lines.greet_again: The same merchant. The piece you took last time, did it sell over the sea, and for what? Tell me true and I will know.
rumour: The law puts a quarter more on a blow to my hand. The harper's too, and the goldsmith's. Somebody once counted what a hand is worth.
The king sends our cloaks to a king in the east, they say, the white, the grey and the blue. I would like to see what comes back.
No grain boat since Easter. I have a chest for my daughter with silver in it. I look at it and I look at the meal bin.
lines.saying: A short cloak well woven is warmer than a long one badly sold.
lines.farewell: Come at shearing. The first cloth off the loom is yours to refuse.

people.source: invented. The oak weaving sword and the pin with inlaid stones are finds from Aalsum; 'the woman who makes fresum' and the higher fine for her hand: Lex Frisionum, judgements of Wlemar. The Frisian cloaks white, grey, red and blue sent to the caliph: Notker II.9 (tr. Grant 1907), paraphrased

people.name: the old Northman
people.trait: Calm, watchful, long past proving anything; a Dane who chose this marsh and was baptised here, and whom the Frisians follow when it comes to fighting.
people.want: His grandchildren left in peace on their mound, speaking Frisian.
people.fear: His own people's sails; and that the Frisians will one day remember what he was before.
people.voice: Few words, Frisian with a Danish edge. He says a small thing and means a large one.
people.looks: Near seventy, big, white hair cropped, a scar through one eyebrow, a Frisian farmer's tunic and short cloak, a wooden cross at his neck, an old good sword kept oiled above the door.
knows: how a Danish lord thinks when he asks for tribute, and what he will take in its place
which sails off the islands are traders and which are not, from the set of the yard
the terms on which beaten men may be let go
tafl, better than anyone on this coast

ties.note: served no lord of the Rhine mouths and was asked to; Rodulf was Rorik's nephew
left Denmark in the old king's time and does not say why
sends his tribute to the count and none to Dorestad
the head of a house on the long mound, who listens when he says how his own people fight

lines.greet: Merchants bring news and leave. That suits me. Sit down. The board is set.
lines.greet_again: You come back to a place with nothing to buy. Either you like my ale or you want to know something.
rumour: Rodulf will come. He has been paid everywhere else, so he thinks paying is the custom of the country.
They asked me what to answer him. I said: tell him whom you owe, and that it is not him. Then sharpen everything.
The ones in the house wanted to live. I said take their silver and their oath. A dead man swears nothing, and his kin come looking.
lines.saying: Cattle die and kinsmen die. I came here to see which goes first.
lines.farewell: If you meet sails from the north, say there is nothing here but mud and a church. It is nearly true.

people.source: Annals of Fulda 873: a Northman, long a Christian and settled among the Frisians, led them when Rodulf was killed, and counselled taking the survivors' treasure and oath. He is real and unnamed; his age, his farm and his reasons are ours (?). His saying turns Hávamál 77 (Bellows 1923)

people.name: Gerbrand
people.trait: Neat, close, proud of a round penny; he has struck a count's name ten thousand times and never seen the count.
people.want: Old silver and foreign silver brought to his hearth, and the dies kept sharp.
people.fear: A light penny laid at his door; and the count's man coming unannounced.
people.voice: Clipped and quiet, counting under his breath. He weighs the question before he answers it.
people.looks: About forty, small, burn-scarred forearms, a leather apron over a good wool tunic, cropped hair, a punch and a little folding scale hung at his belt.
knows: what a Doccinga penny weighs and what it will pass for in the north and the east
which foreign coins are good silver and which are washed
what the skippers take to the Baltic lands and what they bring back
the count's due on every pound struck

ties.note: the wife of the moneyer on the Ems, who strikes for another count; the two houses trade gossip of dies and each calls the other's pennies light

lines.greet: Lay your silver there. Do not tell me what it weighs. The scale has not heard you and will not agree.
lines.greet_again: The merchant with the honest bag. Or the careful one. I have not yet decided which.
rumour: DOCC on one side, BRVN on the other, and the king's head. I am told the count is a tall man. I only know his name fits the die.
A skipper took four hundred of mine east last spring. He says beyond the Baltic they cut them in half to make change. Half my work.
The count is dead on the road, they say, killed. I strike his name until someone brings me a new one. A penny does not mourn.
lines.saying: A thin penny travels further than a fat one. Nobody keeps it.
lines.farewell: Count them at the door, not on the boat. On the boat it is your word against the sea's.

people.source: invented; the coins name only count and place. The pennies: en.numista.com/48388; finds in Scandinavia, the Baltic lands and Russia: Cultuurhistorische verkenning 2008. Bruno killed 26 June 1057: nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruno_II_van_Brunswijk

people.name: Meinbod
people.trait: The smith of the long mound: quick, talkative, generous with a handful, and bad at tallies.
people.want: Bar iron that has not passed through three men's hands; a bell to make, once in his life, instead of hinges.
people.fear: Charcoal: there is not a tree in a day's walk, and every sack comes by boat.
people.voice: Talks while he strikes, and stops both at once to laugh.
people.looks: A short broad man of about forty with a singed red beard, a leather apron over bare arms, a hammer he does not put down to talk.
knows: what iron and charcoal cost on the creek this year
every boat's ironwork between the Lauwers and the Vlie
who on the mounds is building and who is mending
the weight of the church's hinges, which he made

ties.note: the Westergo smith says he sells rivets by the handful and not by the count; he says a handful is a count, for a man with honest hands
made the church's hinges and latch, and is paid in Masses he mostly attends
mends the pilot's boat hooks and hears from him which boats are coming
they were boys on this mound; he made the knife Aldger carries
takes heath iron from the IJssel smith by way of the Almere boats, and is a keg of rivets behind (?)

lines.greet: A boat! She has iron in her or she wants iron on her. Either way you have come to the right fire.
lines.greet_again: Back again. That rudder iron held, then. I said it would. I say that of all of them, but of yours I meant it.
rumour: The smith at Winaldum counts his rivets out one by one, like a priest with beads. I give a handful. Nobody has ever brought a handful back.
No charcoal on the creek since Easter. I am burning peat and old hurdles, and it shows in the weld.
The priest wants a bell. I could cast a bell. I have never cast a bell. Those are two different sentences, he says.
lines.saying: Cold iron and a cold hearth: a marsh smith's two saints.
lines.farewell: Mind the creek bar going out. I have straightened three keel bands this year for men who did not.

people.source: invented, to make real the smith whom wijnaldum.bernrad calls his rival. Smithing waste is common on the terps (Wijnaldum: Besteman et al. 1999); every sack of charcoal and bar of iron had to be brought to the treeless marsh. No smith is recorded at Dokkum (?).

people.name: Aldbern
people.trait: Head of a house on the long mound in the tribute years: slow to anger, exact in memory, the man the district sends when an answer must be given.
people.want: To pay tribute to none but the king, as his fathers swore; and his uncle's pot of silver at Winaldum left where it lies until it is needed.
people.fear: A Dane's counter on the creek bank asking, pleasantly, whether it has been a good year.
people.voice: Says a thing once, in the fewest words, and then waits as long as it takes.
people.looks: A tall spare farmer of forty with a fair beard, a grey cloak pinned with a plain bronze disc, a spear he carries like a staff.
knows: who on the mounds of Oostergo paid Rorik's men and who was paid by them
where the old Northman's farm stands and what he advises
when sails were last seen off the north shore, by the word from Westergo
what his mother's brother at Winaldum has in the ground, though not where

ties.note: his mother's brother, head of the old lords' terp; they send each other word when sails are seen
follows the old Northman's counsel when it comes to fighting, and nobody else's
Rorik's men took tribute here when they could reach it; the Cokingi drove him out in 867, and Aldbern was one of them (?)
holds his land of Saint Martin's, whose bishop has fled; the rent in cheese is put by all the same

lines.greet: You came by Winaldum. Then you have seen my mother's brother's house. If the head house is standing, say only that.
lines.greet_again: The same boat. Good. What did you see off the north shore, and how many?
rumour: We drove the Dane out. The Cokingi, they call us, in the south. He came back with a king's leave, and we have not yet decided about the king.
They are counting on every mound who paid and who was paid. It will take a winter. It is the best kind of counting, done after.
There is an old Northman farming among us who tells us how his own people fight. We listen. He has grandchildren here.
lines.saying: To none but King Louis and his sons. A short answer keeps well.
lines.farewell: If the house at Winaldum stands empty when you next pass, come here first. Before you tell anyone else.

people.source: invented, to make real the 'sister's son at Doccinga' of the story wijnaldum.silver_in_the_sod. The Cokingi who drove Rorik out in 867: Annales Bertiniani 867. The Frisians of Oostergo answering Rodulf in 873 that they owe tribute to none but King Louis and his sons, and the Northman long settled among them who led them: Annales Fuldenses 873.

stories.title: Twelve pennies in a knot
stories.summary: Aldger's mother has kept, unspent for twenty years, the ship's boy's wage he brought home from the voyage that fled York. She means it to be the first silver of the blood-price, if anyone will carry it and see the price named.
stories.picture: A thin old woman in a striped shawl holding out a small knotted cloth on her open palm, grave markers and a grey creek behind her, evening light.

beats.text: Liafhild feeds the crew and asks whether her son keeps the fasts. She shows the knotted cloth and does not say what it is.
At his father's grave Aldger says his father never asked. Liafhild unties the knot: twelve light pennies of the old king. She asks the merchant to carry them over there.
In spring or autumn Liudger is here. He was on the same ship and tells what was said aboard: who struck, and that the boy saw it.
Thiadburg tells the story plainly and will put up part of the price if her son is named in the settlement.
Ecgwulf names the price before the archbishop's man. The twelve old pennies are laid down first, and weighed, and found light.
Aldger stands at the grave and says his own name aloud, and his father's. Liafhild gives the merchant the empty cloth.

endings.how: The merchant carried the twelve pennies to Eoforwic and saw the price paid before witnesses.
endings.text: Aldger walks the strand at Eoforwic under his own name. At home there is a bed kept for the merchant and a place at the board on every feast, for as long as the house on the long mound stands.
endings.reward: Aldger's loyalty for life; free lodging and provision at Doccinga for this merchant and his heirs; Liafhild's word to every mound in Oostergo that the house deals fairly; cloth at Aalsum at the kin price

endings.how: The merchant took the old pennies to a mint and had them changed for new, at the moneyer's loss.
endings.text: The silver is worth a little more and means nothing. Liafhild counts the new coins, gives them back, and does not offer the pot.
endings.reward: A few pennies' gain; Liafhild cool from then on; Aldger says nothing for a week

endings.how: The price was not paid before Liafhild died.
endings.text: She is buried third from the thorn, beside Aldbrand, with the knot in her hand. Aldger asks to be put ashore here for the burying and comes back aboard a day late.
endings.reward: Nothing in silver; the grave can be remembered; a heir may still pay before 813 and have half the welcome

stories.reward: A home port in the north: free lodging, a pilot who does not charge, first refusal of the Aalsum cloth, and a steersman who will not leave the house.

stories.title: The fifth of June
stories.summary: Boniface's day is the one day in the year when this marsh is full: pilgrims, priests, Liudger on his horse, and in 793 priests burned out from beyond the Lauwers with nothing but their oil. The church needs wax and wine carried in, and people carried out.
stories.picture: A crowd climbing a steep green mound to a small plank church, boats crowded on the mud below, a tall tonsured man leading a horse through them, bright windy morning.

beats.text: The bishop's cellarer has wax, wine and oil for Doccinga and no boat to send them in. Pilgrims on the bank ask for passage north.
The feast. Meinward reads the names of the fifty. Liudger preaches in Frisian from the church door because the church will not hold them, then asks the merchant what the sea is saying.
Nine priests from east of the Lauwers sleep in beds for four. One must reach Traiectum to tell the bishop; one means to go back over the river before the leaves turn.
Landric, the island priest, fills a flask at the spring and says that on his father's island the water was drawn in silence. He does not say which he prefers.
A year on, the churches are being raised again. Whoever carried a priest back is remembered there by name.
On the strand under the wall a young priest waits with a chalice, a book and a small bell: the first of those sent back over the Lauwers.

endings.how: The merchant brought the wax and wine by the feast and carried a priest to Traiectum or back over the Lauwers.
endings.text: The church remembers. His name is said on Boniface's day among those who helped, and Liudger knows his face in every port where Liudger is met.
endings.reward: About 60 d from the bishop for the freight; the flag ms_carried_priest; Meinward and Liudger friendly; a prayer for the boat on the fifth of June each year

endings.how: The merchant brought the wine and sold it to the priest at a feast-day price.
endings.text: The feast is kept. Meinward pays, in cheese and the church's few pennies, and thanks him exactly as much as the price deserves.
endings.reward: About 90 d in silver and cheese; Meinward cool; no word carried to Traiectum

endings.how: The merchant did not come, or came after the day.
endings.text: The Mass was said with watered wine and tallow candles. Nobody blames a boat for the wind. The wax is still wanted for All Saints.
endings.reward: Nothing; the order stands at a plain price

stories.reward: The church's goodwill in every Frisian port of the mission, a standing order for wax and wine each May, and Liudger's friendship.

stories.title: A chest for bread
stories.summary: The mound country grows cattle, not corn, and buys its bread every year. In the hungry years the grain boats do not come, and the weaver at Aalsum looks at her daughter's dowry chest and at the meal bin.
stories.picture: A tall woman in a checked gown standing between an open oak chest with silver in it and an empty wooden meal bin, a loom behind her, a girl watching from the door.

beats.text: No grain boat since Easter. Butter and cheese are cheap because nobody can eat them with nothing. Liafhild asks what the merchant has under his deck boards.
Meinhild offers cloth for rye at any fair count. If cloth is not enough, there is the chest: Thiadhild's dowry, in old silver and one gold ring with a red stone.
Meinward has the king's price for a measure of rye from the bishop's letter and reads it aloud. He will witness a sale at that price and write the merchant's name to Traiectum.
Rye is to be had on the dam, dear. Thiadburg sells hers at the king's price and asks where it is going.

endings.how: The merchant sold grain at the king's price and took cloth and cheese for it.
endings.text: The chest stays shut. Thiadhild marries at Martinmas with her dowry whole, and the first cloth off the Aalsum looms each year is kept for the merchant.
endings.reward: A hold of Frisian cloth and cheese worth 80 to 150 d at Dorestad; the flag hy_fed_poor; Meinhild a fast friend; first refusal of the Aalsum cloth

endings.how: The merchant took the dowry silver and the ring for grain at a famine price.
endings.text: The mound eats. The girl does not marry that year. The gold ring with the red stone is the merchant's, and every woman on the coast knows whose it was.
endings.reward: About 200 d in old silver and a gold ring; Meinhild wary; the weavers of Oostergo sell to him last

endings.how: The merchant gave a share of the grain at the church door and sold the rest fairly.
endings.text: Meinward says the merchant's name at Mass beside the bishop's. The poor of four mounds carry his cargo down to the boat for nothing, and it is good cargo.
endings.reward: Less silver than a fair sale by 30 d or so; the deed gave_alms; the flag hy_fed_poor; porters free at this landing for good

stories.reward: The Aalsum weavers as a standing source of the best Frisian cloth, or their silver once.

stories.title: The mound's share
stories.summary: In the summer of 810 two hundred Danish ships lie on the islands, three fights are lost, and the Frisians must find a hundred pounds of silver by weight. Every mound is told its share, and Doccinga has cattle and cloth but little silver.
stories.picture: Farmers and a priest around a folding scale on an upturned tub on the long mound, a few coins and a brooch in the pan, cattle being driven inland behind them, smoke far off over the sea.

beats.text: Radbrand has counted sails off the north shore that are nobody's kin. If the merchant brought warning from the south, the cattle are already inland and the church plate is under a byre floor.
The share is named. Pins, rings and the church's two silver cups are weighed and it is still short. They ask what the merchant has aboard, and on what terms.
Meinward will witness a loan and write the tally on wood: so much silver now, so much cloth at shearing for three years. He will not swear on the altar for a usurer's rate.
The same counting on every mound to the Ems. Men ask which merchants gave, which lent, and which sailed.
The Danish king is dead by his own man's hand and there is peace on the Eider. The loan is still owed; the cloth comes at shearing.

endings.how: The merchant gave silver toward the share and asked nothing.
endings.text: The share is met and the ships go. Doccinga has nothing to give back that year but its word, which it gives in every Frisian port.
endings.reward: The flag gf_paid_share: the Danish fleet lets him be that season; standing in Frisia up; the deed gave_alms; Aalsum cloth at cost for five years

endings.how: The merchant lent the silver against cloth at shearing, witnessed by the priest.
endings.text: The tally stick is split and each keeps half. For three years the first cloth of the mound is his, and they pay to the last ell, without warmth.
endings.reward: The flag gf_paid_share; Frisian cloth worth about 300 d over three years for 150 d lent; the deed fair_dealing if the rate was the priest's

endings.how: The merchant kept his silver and put to sea.
endings.text: The share is met short and made up in cattle at the Danes' own count. Nobody on the long mound says anything to him afterwards; they sell him butter at the stranger's price.
endings.reward: His silver kept; Liafhild and Meinhild cool; no pilot offers himself at this landing for a year

stories.reward: A season's safety from the fleet and the standing of a man who paid, or three years of cloth at a lender's price.

stories.title: To none but King Louis
stories.summary: In June 873 Rodulf, a baptised Dane who has taken tribute along every coast, sends to Oostergo for his. The Frisians answer that they owe it to none but King Louis and his sons, and an old Northman who farms among them tells them how to fight.
stories.picture: A big white-haired man in a Frisian farmer's tunic standing in the door of a plank building with his sword point down, beaten men inside holding out bags and arm-rings, Frisians with spears around the mound, low red sun.

beats.text: The old Northman plays tafl with the merchant and asks, as if it did not matter, where Rodulf's ships were last seen and how many.
Rodulf's men have come and named a sum. The men of the district give their answer before the priest: tribute to none but King Louis and his sons. Count Albdag is sent for.

Rodulf is dead with hundreds of his men. The rest are shut in a building and want to live. The old Northman says: take their treasure and their oath. There is more silver than the mounds can count, and no boat to carry word south but one.
The news is worth a great deal to whoever brings it first: to the bishop, and to every merchant who has paid Rodulf.

endings.how: The merchant carried the word south before anyone else.
endings.text: At Traiectum he is heard by the bishop the same day. The annals write that Rodulf ended a dog's life with the death it deserved; the merchant's name is not in them, but it is in the count's memory.
endings.reward: About 120 d in gifts for the news; standing with the count and the bishop; prices move in his favour at the next port because he knows first

endings.how: The merchant weighed and carried the Northmen's treasure for the district, for a share.
endings.text: The treasure is weighed on his scale before the priest and the count's man, a tenth is his for the weighing and the carrying, and the rest goes to the church and the mounds.
endings.reward: A tenth of the weighed silver, about 250 d; the deed fair_dealing; the old Northman a fast friend

endings.how: The merchant was elsewhere, or would not land while Danes were ashore.
endings.text: He hears it at the next port from a man who heard it from another. This year a skipper from Doccinga is given the best berth wherever Frisians meet.

stories.reward: First word of the biggest news of the year, or a tenth of a raider's hoard honestly weighed.

works.name: A bell for Boniface's church
works.what: A small bell of riveted iron sheet dipped in bronze, hung in a frame by the church door, so that the hours and the feasts can be heard across the marsh and a boat in fog can find the mound.
works.picture: Two men hoisting a hand-high dark bell into a timber frame beside a plank church, the priest steadying it, marsh and sea behind.
works.needs: The priest friendly; the bell bought on the Rhine and carried here, or the silver to send for one
works.gives: The priest and Liudger remember the giver; in fog the landing can be found by ear; the giver's name is said on the fifth of June
works.source: Liudger wants a bell for the Frisians: the spine, cast.liudger. Small hand bells of iron sheet brazed with bronze are the mission's kind in these years (?). The price is the game's

works.name: A brushwood landing
works.what: Bundles of alder and willow pegged into the mud in a strip from the creek to the foot of the long mound, with planks laid over, so that a boat can be loaded dry-shod at half tide.
works.picture: Men in the mud to their thighs pegging down bundles of brushwood in a line from a beached boat to a low green mound.
works.needs: Timber and brushwood brought in by boat: the marsh has no wood. The pilot's goodwill
works.gives: Loading takes less of the tide; no porters needed for small cargo; the house's own place at the landing
works.source: No landing has been found: Cultuurhistorische verkenning 2008. Brushwood and plank staging is the common harbour work of the coast in these years; here it is ours (?)

works.name: A curb for the spring
works.what: An oak curb and a lid for the spring on the church mound, with a trough below for pilgrims and beasts, in a country where sweet water is short.
works.picture: A square oak frame set round a small clear pool beside a church, a woman lowering a dipper, pilgrims waiting with flasks.
works.needs: Oak planks carried from the Rhine; the priest's leave
works.gives: Water for the boat without charge; the giver may fill casks here before any other skipper; a small standing with the church
works.source: Willibald ch. 9: sweet water is scarce in almost all Frisia, and the spring on the mound. The curb is ours

works.name: A pilgrims' house
works.what: A turf-walled house with a hearth and benches for twenty on the lee of the church mound, where those who come for the fifth of June can sleep dry and a sick traveller can lie.
works.picture: A long low turf house with smoke at the roof under the church mound, pilgrims with staffs at the door, a priest handing in a pot.
works.needs: The church's leave and its ground; roof timber by boat; one season of the mound's labour, paid in grain
works.gives: More pilgrims, so more buyers at the landing in May and June; the house's crew lodge and are healed free; the bishop at Traiectum hears of it
works.source: Guests to be received as Christ: Rule of Benedict ch. 53. Pilgrims on 5 June are likely and not recorded (?); the canons' and pilgrims' church is of the 11th century: Cultuurhistorische verkenning 2008

works.name: A length of the sea dike
works.what: A share in the first low dike of sods along the creek, a rod's length for every share, so the pasture behind stays dry through the winter tides.
works.picture: A line of men and women with sod-spades and hand-barrows raising a low green bank along a creek, the tuff church half built on the mound behind.
works.needs: The year 1000 or after; standing with the men of the district, who share out the lengths
works.gives: A plot of dry pasture behind the dike in the house's name, with its yearly rent in butter and cheese; a voice when the district meets
works.source: The first sea dikes along the creek come in the 11th century: Cultuurhistorische verkenning 2008. Shares by length are the later Frisian custom, set back here (?)

ships.how: bought second-hand from a farmer, or built in a fortnight from planks you bring
ships.note: Every mound keeps a flat boat for the creeks, for fetching hay and ferrying cattle. There is no timber here: the wood must come by water.
ships.picture: A flat tarred punt on the mud beside a hay rick, a pole laid across it.
ships.source: The creeks of the unembanked marsh: Cultuurhistorische verkenning 2008; the class from ship_classes_793.json

ships.note: A small clinker boat of the house's own kind now and then stands for sale on the landing when a farmer's son gives up the sea. Riveted clinker boats were at home on this coast.
ships.picture: A small clinker boat propped on the mud with a hazel branch tied to her stem to show she is for sale.
ships.source: Rivets of clinker boats in the Frisian mounds, 400 to 800: Design/content/ships.md [BJM]. No ship find at Dokkum

ships.note: Once there is a market and a mint, skippers of this place sail to the Baltic lands, and an old sea trader can sometimes be had from a widow. None is built here: no oak.
ships.picture: A broad old trading ship lying on her bilge at the ebb below a market mound, her mast unstepped, a woman and a buyer looking her over.
ships.source: Dokkum pennies in Scandinavia, the Baltic lands and Russia show the reach of its skippers: Cultuurhistorische verkenning 2008. That hulls were sold here is ours (?)

sayings.text: A Frisian trusts God and the mound, and builds the mound first.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the mound raised before the church: Willibald ch. 9

sayings.text: They looked for gold and found books. So they were not the last.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, after Willibald ch. 8

sayings.text: Sunday work: four solidi here, twelve beyond the Lauwers. Mend your net on this bank.
sayings.source: Lex Frisionum XVIII, turned into a joke; the fines are the law's

sayings.text: What use is a cloak that will not cover you in bed, nor keep the rain off on a horse? In this marsh: it does not drag in the mud.
sayings.source: The king's complaint of the short Frisian cloaks: Notker, Gesta Karoli I.34 (tr. Grant 1907), paraphrased; the answer is invented

sayings.text: He drew his foot back from the font to stay with his fathers. We put ours in, and kept the fathers anyway.
sayings.source: The story of King Radbod at the font (Vita Vulframni, LATER), as the spine gives it for a Frisian; the turn is invented

sayings.text: Cattle die, and kinsmen die, and so one dies one's self; but a noble name will never die, if good renown one gets.
sayings.source: Hávamál 77 (tr. Bellows 1923), said by the old Northman after 850

sayings.text: This year the heathen men asked tribute of the eastern district, and were answered that it was owed to the king and to no other. And they had their answer twice.
sayings.source: invented in the Chronicle's voice; the fact is the Annals of Fulda 873

sayings.text: Who robs a shrine is taken to the sand the tide covers and given to the gods he robbed. Since the priests came we fine him instead. He is said to prefer it.
sayings.source: Lex Frisionum, Additio sapientum XI; the last two sentences invented

sayings.text: Though baptised, he ended a dog's life with the death it deserved.
sayings.source: Annals of Xanten 873 on Rodulf, paraphrased from en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodulf_Haraldsson

sayings.text: I walk where the sea was this morning and sail where the cattle stood. What am I? A man of this country.
sayings.source: invented riddle in the manner of the Exeter Book; the tides over the marsh: Willibald ch. 9

easter_eggs.text: The mound was raised in one piece, three to four times a man's height of salt-marsh sods, where ordinary mounds grow a layer at a time over generations. Radbrand will say it is the only thing in the district finished in the year it was begun.

Adelsuit swears the book he held up was a gospel book. A monk who has seen the slashed book kept at Fulda will say, if asked, that it holds tracts against heresy and no gospels. Both can be told the other's version; neither gives way.

The spring came because a servant's horse sank to its forelegs while the count rode round his new mound. King Pippin had the story from men who saw it, Bishop Lul from the king, and the writer from Lul: ask Meinward and he gives the same chain of names.
At Aalsum a woman wears a gold ring with a red stone and a bronze pin set with small stones, and beats her weft with an oak sword. All three will lie in that mound for a thousand years.
A clerk writing about this place puts down 'Dockynchirica': Dokkum church. To the people who write, the church is the place.
easter_eggs.source: a 9th-century text, perhaps the Life of Willehad (?): nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dokkum

easter_eggs.text: Willehad, an Englishman, began here before he crossed the Lauwers, where they cast lots on whether to kill him and the lot let him live. His day, the eighth of November, is kept by one old priest and nobody else.
After 1038, a skipper home from far beyond the Baltic says he saw a Doccinga penny on a string round a child's neck, in a country where they have never heard of the count, the king or the marsh.
easter_eggs.source: Dokkum pennies found in Scandinavia, the Baltic lands and Russia; one shown among Finland's finds (?): Cultuurhistorische verkenning 2008; Finnish National Museum page, seen only as a search result

easter_eggs.text: Strike a harper's hand, a goldsmith's or a weaver's and the fine is a quarter higher than for anyone else's. Meinhild can say the clause by heart and holds up the hand while she does.

On Saint Stephen's day 838 the sea came over everything but the mounds. A boat was the one thing that floated. If the house had a boat at this landing that winter, people here still know whose cattle it carried.

unlocks.what: a home in the north: a bed, a board and a welcome on the long mound
unlocks.how: End 'Twelve pennies in a knot' with the blood-price paid, or feed the mound fairly in a hungry year
unlocks.gives: lodge and provision at Doccinga cost nothing; morale up each time she lies here; the welcome passes to the heirs at half strength

unlocks.what: the creek marks of Oostergo, taught by Radbrand
unlocks.how: Hire him as pilot three times and pay what he asks without haggling, or bring him news of the Danish ships before 810
unlocks.gives: no pilot needed between the Vlie and the Lauwers; the landing can be made at half tide; he tells what ships have come and gone for nothing

unlocks.what: first refusal of the Aalsum cloth each year at shearing
unlocks.how: End 'A chest for bread' with the dowry chest shut, or lend fairly in 810
unlocks.gives: Frisian cloth bought at source at the kin price, before any other skipper, each June

unlocks.what: the house's name said at Mass on the fifth of June
unlocks.how: Fund the bell, or bring the wax and wine for the feast and carry a priest
unlocks.gives: standing with the church in every Frisian port of the mission; the priest's letter of good name to Traiectum; the flag ms_carried_priest if a priest was carried

unlocks.what: a place as witness when Adelsuit swears before the bishop's clerk
unlocks.how: Hear her story on three visits before 820, then be at the spring when the clerk from Traiectum comes, between 820 and 836
unlocks.gives: the deed carried_letters if the merchant takes the clerk's leaves to Traiectum; the bishop's thanks; her last line, said only once

unlocks.what: a hearing by the Frisian lot instead of a feud
unlocks.how: Be friendly with the priest and bring a quarrel between crewmen or with a Frisian skipper to the clergy house
unlocks.gives: a lawsuit here ends in one day by the two twigs; won_case or lost_case, with no kin coming after either man

unlocks.what: the old Northman's reading of a Danish sail
unlocks.how: Sit with him and play tafl on three visits between 850 and 873
unlocks.gives: at sea off Frisia, a raider's sail is told from a trader's a little sooner; he vouches for the merchant to baptised Danes

unlocks.what: new Doccinga pennies at the moneyer's own count
unlocks.how: Bring Gerbrand old or foreign silver three times between 1038 and 1057 and take his weight without argument
unlocks.gives: coin changed here at a smaller loss; a bag of thin pennies that pass well in the Baltic lands

unlocks.what: The old Northman's reading of a sail, as the cards give it
unlocks.how: Play tafl with him until he is friendly, between 850 and 872, and ask (the card harbour.tafl_at_the_farm.doccinga).
unlocks.gives: flag rf_northmans_word: the unlock doccinga.northmans_word in the engine's own flag
